intro: Image to Base64 turns an image into text so you can put it straight into the code of a web page, a stylesheet, an email template or a JSON file, without hosting it separately. It is the usual approach for small icons, email signature logos, test images or assets that must live inside a single HTML file.

It accepts JPG, PNG, WEBP, GIF, SVG, AVIF, BMP and ICO. The image is not recompressed or changed: its original bytes are encoded, so quality and transparency are exactly the same. The MIME type (image/png, image/svg+xml…) is detected from the file's content, not its extension, so the browser shows it correctly even if the name is wrong.

Choose the text format: a full data URI (data:image/…;base64,…), ready for a src attribute or url(); just the Base64, if your program adds the rest; a CSS rule with background-image; or an HTML img tag with an empty alt attribute, which you should fill in with a description. The result appears on screen with a “Copy” button and you can also download it as a TXT file.

The conversion runs in your browser, without uploading the image. You can convert several at once and get all the TXT files in a ZIP. If together they go over 200,000 characters, the ones that do not fit on screen are offered only as a file, with a notice, so the page does not freeze.
steps: Pick the format: data URI, Base64 only, CSS or HTML.
Press “Start”, then copy the text with the “Copy” button or download the TXT.

faq.q: Why is the text bigger than the image?
faq.a: Base64 represents every 3 bytes with 4 characters, so the result is roughly a third larger than the original file. That is why it pays off with small images; for large photos it is better to link the normal file.

faq.q: Can I make it smaller before converting?
faq.a: Yes, and it is a good idea. Run the image through Compress image or Resize image, or turn it into WEBP with Convert image, then generate the Base64 of the result here.

It depends on the email program: quite a few block or do not show data URI images, especially webmail and corporate clients. For bulk emails, linking an image hosted on a website is usually more reliable.
